sentences.text: Picture two fields growing the same crop, one farmed organically and one not. At harvest, does the organic field come up short, and by how much?
Ask around and you hear both answers with total confidence: organic grows less, or organic grows just as much.
And the answer sets up a second question: if organic does grow less, is it still the greener choice?
AsapSCIENCE told its viewers that "organic crop yields are 25% lower on average than conventional ones".
Mark Hyman says the opposite: "you can grow as much food or more food better food without all those chemicals".
So who is right?

A meta-analysis by Lauren Ponisio and colleagues pooled side-by-side yield comparisons and found organic yields 19.2% lower than conventional, with a likely range of 15.5 to 22.9%, and the authors warn that even this may overstate the gap, because the published studies lean towards reporting bigger conventional wins.
Conventional came out ahead for every crop type the study grouped, and for most of those types the gap was about the same size.
That gap is real, but it is smaller than the ones earlier meta-analyses had reported.

Why lower at all? A review of organic food and health, citing earlier work, points to fertiliser: in organic systems crop yield is typically limited by how much nitrogen the plants can get, which is not the case in conventional systems.
Not everyone agrees: a clinical report for pediatricians says well-designed farming studies show organic yields comparable to conventional farming.
But in the report's summary, the part we could read, that is one sentence, with no yield figure and no studies named.
So on the pooled data, yes: organic fields grew less, by roughly a fifth or perhaps a little less, but where crops were rotated or grown in mixtures the gap shrank to about 8 or 9%.
Which raises the next question: if each organic field grows less, does organic need more land for the same food, and does that undo its green reputation?
Harvard Health put it plainly: "Organic foods are clearly healthier for the planet".
The same pediatric report agrees, saying organic farming "has been demonstrated to have less environmental impact than conventional approaches".
But a meta-analysis by Clark and Tilman measured the impacts per unit of food, not per field, using studies that assessed both systems within the same publication.
Measured that way, organic systems needed 25 to 110% more land.
They used 15% less energy, but had 37% higher eutrophication potential, a measure of nutrient pollution.
Greenhouse gas emissions came out similar, because relying on manure turns more of a farm's nitrogen into nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas.
The authors add that these are comparisons at a local scale, and the picture might differ regionally, nationally or globally.
And they warn against reading this as a win for conventional farming, which uses more energy and relies on high fertiliser, herbicide and pesticide inputs that can harm health and the environment.

What does dwarf the organic question is the food itself: on every indicator they examined, ruminant meats had 20 to 100 times the impacts of plant-based foods, a difference far larger than the one between farming systems.
So per unit of food, organic is not clearly greener: it trades lower energy use for more land and more nutrient pollution, with emissions about even.
The next time a label or a video says organic grows just as much, ask which studies, and how many.
And when something is sold as better for the planet, ask: better per what? Per plate of food, the answer here was mixed.
